carnival.note: In the US, a carnival is also a traveling fair with rides and games.
ex: Our town has a big carnival every February.
We wore masks and bright costumes to the carnival.
Are you going to the carnival parade on Saturday?
Music and dancing filled the streets during the carnival.

rehab.note: Informal; usually no article: "go to rehab," "be in rehab."
ex: He went to rehab to stop drinking.
She spent two months in rehab last year.
The rehab center is outside the city.
Is your brother still in rehab for drugs?

dime.note: A US or Canadian coin worth ten cents.
ex: I found a dime under the couch cushion.
A dime is worth ten cents in the US.
Can you lend me a dime for the parking meter?
I need two dimes and a quarter for the machine.

marshal.note: Most often a marshal is a US police officer or an official at an event: "a fire marshal."

ex: We only buy organic vegetables at the market.
Is organic food really better for your health?
The farm near our town grows organic apples.
She prefers organic milk for her kids.
The elf in the story had pointed ears.
She dressed up as an elf for Christmas.
In this game, you can play as an elf.
Elves live in the forest in many old stories.

barrel.note: Also a big round container for wine or water, and the tube of a gun.
ex: Oil prices rose to ninety dollars a barrel.
The country produces a million barrels a day.
The price of a barrel of oil fell.
How many liters are in one barrel of oil?

disc.note: "Disc" is usual for CDs and DVDs; "disk" for computer disks.

ex: A hacker stole thousands of passwords from the site.
Hackers attacked the bank's website last night.
He used to be a hacker as a teen.
Use a strong password to protect your account from hackers.

spray.note: Also a verb: "spray the plants." It can mean small drops of water: "sea spray."
ex: Use bug spray before you go camping.
She bought a can of hair spray.
This cleaning spray smells like lemons.
Can you recommend a good spray for a sore throat?

mhm.note: Informal; used in speaking or chat to mean "yes" or "I'm listening."

organism.note: For the human body, say "body": "Sleep is good for your body."
ex: Bacteria are tiny organisms that live almost everywhere.
Every living organism needs water and energy.
The lake is full of small living organisms.
Scientists found a new organism deep in the ocean.

gallon.note: Used mainly in the US; one gallon is about 3.8 liters.
ex: Gas costs four dollars a gallon.
We bought a gallon of milk.
Our car's tank holds about fifteen gallons.
Drink half a gallon of water a day.

scan.note: Often a verb: "scan the code." Also a medical test: "a brain scan."
ex: Send me a scan of your passport, please.
Can you make a scan of this document?
I saved the scan as a PDF file.
The scan of the contract is in your email.

franc.note: Today the franc is used mainly in Switzerland.
ex: The Swiss franc is a very stable currency.
Lunch in Zurich cost us thirty francs.
France used the franc before the euro.
How many francs do I get for one hundred dollars?

ring.note: Most often a "ring" is jewelry for your finger, or a verb: "The phone is ringing."

nim.note: Usually a name. As a word, nim is a math game: players take turns taking objects from piles.
ex: Nim is a game for two players with small objects.
In nim, each player takes some stones from a pile.
Our math teacher showed us how to play nim.
The player who takes the last stone wins at nim.

solo.note: Also means "alone": "She traveled solo," "a solo album."
ex: She played a long guitar solo at the concert.
The drum solo was the best part of the show.
He sang a solo in the school show.
Can you play the piano solo for us again?

player.note: Most often a "player" is a person who plays a sport or game: "a tennis player."

tag.note: Often a small label: "a price tag," "a name tag." Also a verb: "tag a friend."

ex: What genre of music do you like best?
Jazz is my favorite music genre.
She writes books in many different genres.
Horror is a very popular genre with teenagers.
We went snorkeling on the coral reef.
The reef is full of colorful fish.
Our boat almost hit a reef near the island.
Is it safe to swim near the reef?

shot.note: Most often "shot" means firing a gun, a try, or a vaccine: "a flu shot."
ex: Let's order a round of shots for everyone.
He drank a shot of tequila at the bar.
Two shots of vodka are enough for me tonight.
Can we get three shots of tequila, please?

distress.note: Uncountable: a lot of distress (not "a distress").
ex: She was in great distress after the bad news.
The loud noise caused the dog a lot of distress.
Call a doctor if the patient shows signs of distress.
Talking to a friend can help reduce emotional distress.

jeep.note: "Jeep" is also a brand; for any such car say "SUV" or "four-wheel drive".
ex: We drove an old jeep through the desert.
The jeep got stuck in the mud.
He rented a jeep for the mountain trip.
The soldiers rode in an open army jeep.

clip.note: Also a small thing that holds things: "a paper clip." A song's video is a "music video."

musical.note: Most often "musical" is an adjective: "musical instruments," "a musical family."
ex: We saw a great musical in the city theater.
She sang in the school musical last spring.
The musical has some really great songs.
Do you want to see a musical this weekend?

alpha.note: Also a first test version ("alpha version") and a leader ("alpha male").

ex: She became a superstar after her first album.
The superstar signed autographs for his fans.
He is a soccer superstar in his country.
Everyone wanted a photo with the superstar.

drill.note: Also a practice exercise: "a fire drill." As a verb: "drill a hole."
ex: He used a drill to make a hole in the wall.
Can I borrow your drill this weekend?
This old drill is very loud.
She bought a new electric drill at the store.
My daughter put stickers on her notebook.
His laptop is covered with funny stickers.
Remove the price sticker before you give the gift.
The teacher gave him a gold sticker for good work.

badge.note: Often a police badge or a small pin. A card with your name is often a "name tag."
ex: Please wear your badge at all times.
Show your badge at the entrance, please.
The guard at the door checked my badge.
I lost my badge on the first day of the conference.

coaching.note: Often about sports: "The team needs better coaching." Uncountable.
ex: She offers career coaching to young managers online.
Coaching helped him become a better manager.
The company pays for coaching for its team leaders.
Do you think life coaching really works?

madame.note: In English "madam" is more common; "madame" sounds French.
ex: "Madame, your table is ready," said the waiter.
"Good evening, madame," the hotel worker said politely.
Excuse me, madame, is this your bag?
The waiter asked, "Would madame like some coffee?"

cement.note: Uncountable: some cement, a bag of cement (not "a cement").
ex: The workers mixed the cement with sand and water.
The cement needs a full day to dry.
We bought ten bags of cement for the garage.
Is the floor in the basement made of cement?

gin.note: Uncountable: some gin, a glass of gin; in a bar, "a gin" means one drink.
ex: He ordered a gin and tonic at the bar.
This gin tastes a bit like pine trees.
Add a little lime to your gin.
She doesn't drink gin or whiskey.

auto.note: Mostly used before other words: "auto parts." In everyday speech, people say "car."
ex: He works in an auto repair shop.
The auto industry is growing fast this year.
Auto insurance is very expensive in this city.
She bought auto parts online for her old car.

disk.note: "Disk" is usual for computers; for CDs and DVDs, "disc" is more common.

ex: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen.
Hydrogen is the lightest gas in the world.
This new bus runs on hydrogen instead of diesel.
The sun is made mostly of hydrogen.

kris.note: Most often "Kris" is a first name. A kris is a wavy dagger from Indonesia.
ex: A kris is a small dagger with a wavy blade.
The museum has an old kris from Indonesia.
He bought a kris as a gift on his trip.
The kris hangs on the wall in their living room.
She has worked in banking for ten years.
Mobile banking is fast and easy.
He chose a career in banking.
This app makes online banking simple and safe.

terminal.note: As an adjective, "terminal" means causing death: "a terminal illness."

HR.note: Short for "human resources," the department that hires people. Usually no article: "talk to HR."

reserve.note: Often a verb: "reserve a table." A nature reserve is a protected area for animals.
